documents.title: Academic Integrity (Policy 6Hx28:8-11)
documents.stance_why: The policy's only AI statement treats a submission "generated by Artificial Intelligence (AI)" as cheating "unless the use of AI has been explicitly permitted", so AI is banned unless permitted. It offers no tiers and sets no permitted uses itself, while faculty communicate conditions per course. Restrict fits because permission is the exception.
documents.summary: Valencia College's general academic integrity policy (effective Dec 2023) defines plagiarism, cheating and related violations and sets faculty-led penalties and procedures. AI appears once, as an example of cheating when AI-generated work is submitted without explicit permission. Everything else is general integrity procedure that applies to AI by extension.

units.why: The sentence lists AI-generated submissions as cheating "unless the use of AI has been explicitly permitted", so the default is a ban with explicit permission as the only exception. This is a fallback rule for silence, hence P06 rather than P01 (a flat ban) or P04 (no per-instructor choice is stated here).
units.anchor: generated by Artificial Intelligence (AI), unless the use of AI has been explicitly permitted
units.policy: Submitting an assignment generated by AI is cheating unless the use of AI has been explicitly permitted.
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded phase general with a normalized policy; coder B coded phase during-work with policy null. Both chose P06, actor student, must-not, restrict. The source (Procedures I.B.3) reads 'Submission of an assignment ... generated by Artificial Intelligence (AI), unless the use of AI has been explicitly permitted' as an example of cheating. The rule governs submitting assignment work, so during-work fits better than general (definitions/scope). The anchor alone lacks its subject, so A's normalized policy is kept; it adds nothing beyond the source. A's fit_note about overlap with P19 is kept.
units.fit_note: The text does not mention syllabus silence; it sets AI-generated work as prohibited unless explicitly permitted, which also overlaps P19.

units.why: The same item places AI-generated submission under the heading "Cheating", a form of dishonesty, so unauthorized AI work is academic misconduct. P36 fits because it classifies the act; the explicit-permission fallback is coded separately as P06.
units.anchor: A form of dishonesty in which a student misrepresents their mastery of the course content
units.policy: Submitting an assignment generated by AI without explicit permission is an example of cheating, a form of dishonesty in which a student misrepresents their mastery of the course content.
units.fit_note: The policy names AI only in one example item under cheating; the classification is general and the AI link comes from example 3. The anchor alone is the definition; the AI example is item 3 beneath the list header.
units.resolution_why: Coder A anchored on the list header 'Examples of cheating include but are not limited to:' with policy null and unit_stance neutral; coder B anchored on the definition of cheating with null policy and unit_stance restrict. Both gave P36, student, when-misuse, informs. The source defines cheating (I.B) and lists AI-generated work without permission as item 3, so classifying the AI act as cheating is the rule. B's anchor does not mention AI, so a normalized policy is written from the definition plus item 3. Unit_stance restrict because the classification marks unpermitted AI work as a violation. A's note that the AI example sits in item 3 is merged into fit_note.

units.why: Faculty must communicate "conditions for student work", including "assistance", in each course assessment, which is the route by which AI permission is made explicit; AI is not named, so P09 fits only partly. Chosen over P04 because it is a duty to communicate, not a statement that instructors decide.

units.fit_note: Covers collaboration, assistance, citation and sources in general; AI is not named, but the AI exception depends on explicit permission.
